title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–13)
hook: the Our Father, a friend at midnight, ask, seek, knock

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventy-two went out two by two with one sentence for every door. Your line was peace be to this house. Where did it land? Day four hundred sixty-one.

It's midnight. A friend of yours has shown up after a long trip, hungry, and your kitchen is empty. Not a crust. So you walk next door and knock. From inside, your neighbor groans: the door's locked, the kids are asleep in the bed with me, I can't get up. You knock again. Jesus tells this little comedy right after his disciples ask him for something. Today, what they asked, and why he answers with a man knocking at midnight.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AN EMPTY KITCHEN.` → `THE KIDS ARE ASLEEP. GO AWAY.` → `YOU KNOCK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Luke sets the scene simply. Jesus is praying somewhere, and when he stops, one of his disciples says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John had given his followers a way to pray. Now Jesus gives his. Luke's version of the Our Father is shorter than Matthew's, the one Catholics say at Mass. The Catechism notes the difference: Luke gives five petitions, Matthew seven. Luke's begins simply with Father, then hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us our daily bread, forgive us our sins as we forgive, and lead us not into temptation. Then, right away, the midnight friend. Jesus says: even if the neighbor won't get up because you're his friend, "yet, because of his importunity, he will rise, and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity means pestering. The Greek word is even bolder: shamelessness. The man gets bread because he won't stop knocking. Then the promise: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." And one last picture: which father, if his son asks for a fish, hands him a snake? If you, imperfect as you are, give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him. Notice where the promise ends. Not with whatever you ask for, but with the good Spirit. In Luke, prayer looks like shameless knocking at the door of a Father who wants to give.
screen: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.` · `LUKE'S SHORTER OUR FATHER.` · `IMPORTUNITY: SHAMELESS KNOCKING.` · `HOW MUCH MORE THE GOOD SPIRIT.` · then, large: `KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask once more for something. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've asked for before and given up on: healing for someone, a change in yourself, an answer that never came. Let it come back to mind without embarrassment. The man in the story wasn't embarrassed. If you pray, ask for it again, plainly, one more time, and then ask for the good Spirit too. If you don't pray, hold the hope out in front of you again for a moment, as if you were knocking on a door. The bell holds the time.
importunity. The shameless pestering that got the midnight friend his bread, after the disciples asked Jesus, teach us to pray. Today's word.
Your line: knock. Today, whatever you have quietly stopped asking for, ask one more time, plainly, like a neighbor at midnight. Day four hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass and at the start of each decade of the rosary; the Catechism devotes its final section to the prayer, comparing Luke's five petitions with Matthew's seven.

myth: the disciples asked to be taught, as John taught his disciples
Luke 11:1. John had taught his own disciples to pray.
Luke's Our Father is the same length as the one said at Mass
Luke's is shorter: five petitions. the Mass uses Matthew's seven.
Luke promises that God gives exactly what we ask for
he promises the good Spirit to those who ask.

fork.setup: it's midnight, your guest is hungry, and your neighbor says go away, we're all in bed. what does the man in the story do?
options: keep knocking until he gets up.
fork.reveal: he keeps knocking. Jesus says the neighbor gets up because of his importunity, his shameless persistence.

trapdoor: what you thought: ask, seek, knock means God is a vending machine.
what it means: Jesus tells his friends to pray with shameless persistence to a Father who wants to give, and promises above all the Holy Spirit.
what a scholar hears: the Greek anaideia means shamelessness, a sharper word than the old English importunity.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut unsourced background ("one-room village house", "teachers in that world often gave their followers a prayer") from hook, teach and myth; restored the Douay comma in 11:8 ("yet, because"); softened the closing claim to what Luke 11:13 says; corrected the old note about the Douay's Luke 11:2-4 (the Vulgate and Douay already give the short form there).

Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 11:1, 11:8 and 11:9. The Challoner Douay of Luke 11:2–4 follows the Clementine Vulgate's short form (Father, hallowed be thy name...), matching the five petitions in the voice and CCC 2759. Confirm.
Petitions in the voice are paraphrased, not quoted.
Anaideia = shamelessness is standard lexicon (BDAG); confirm.
Luke 11:13 'the good Spirit' (Douay); paraphrased in the voice.
